sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.

sections.content: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing pretrained teachers iterative sampling process into few network evaluations. Introduction Diffusion and Flow models [2, 19, 30, 31, 53] have emerged as powerful approach to generative modeling, particularly for images [10, 26, 27, 45, 57, 58] and video [1, 3, 25, 39, 55, 60], with growing applications to text [43]. Their sampling process progressively transforms noise into data sample through sequence of denoising steps, typically requiring many neural network evaluations. Diffusion distillation aims to reduce this computational burden by training student to generate samples in one or few steps [4, 47 49, 54, 61, 62]. However, noisy state can correspond to many plausible clean samples, while conventional denoiser provides only single estimate. This raises fundamental question: what information about the teachers generative distribution should few-step student preserve? Existing diffusion distillation methods differ in what they seek to preserve from the teacher. Trajectory-based approaches aim to preserve the teachers sampling process with fewer evaluations. These include progressive distillation [48], which compresses successive denoising steps, consistency distillation [54], which learns mappings to trajectory endpoints, and flow-map distillation [4, 47], which learns transitions between noise levels. Distribution-based approaches, in contrast, seek to preserve the teachers generated distribution without requiring the student to follow the same sampling trajectories. Among them, Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [61, 62] aligns noiseperturbed student and teacher distributions through scorebased objectives, while Moment Matching (MM) [49] enforces agreement between conditional expectations of clean samples at intermediate noisy states. Matching generated distributions does not necessarily preserve the relationship between noisy inputs and clean samples. student may reproduce the teachers overall output distribution while learning different conditional distribution at each noise level [61, 62]. This limitation is particularly relevant to Distribution Matching Distillation, which uses an approximate reverse-KL objective to align noiseperturbed student and teacher distributions. The modeseeking nature of reverse KL can favor dominant modes at the expense of less frequent outcomes, potentially reducing sample diversity [32, 59]. Conditional supervision offers an alternative [8]. Moment Matching compares the students and teachers conditional means, but does so at new noisy state constructed from the students prediction, rather than directly at its original input [49]. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), distribution-based distillation method that trains stochastic student to recover the teachers conditional distribution of clean samples at each noise level. PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. In practice, stochasticity is introduced by simFigure 2. Tilt=Shift Identity. (Left) Estimating tilted posterior mean requires multiple stochastic reverse-diffusion trajectories from the same noisy state, followed by exponential reweighting of the resulting clean samples. (Right) Under Gaussian corruption, the same mean is obtained with single frozen-teacher evaluation at shifted noisy input. ply doubling the first layers input features, and each tilted mean is estimated using as few as four student evaluations per noisy state. The choice of exponential weights is deliberate: under Gaussian corruption, exponentially reweighting the posterior is equivalent to shifting the noisy input at the same noise level [20, 38, 4042], an elementary identity we call the Tilt=Shift Identity. As illustrated in Fig. 2, this identity allows each target mean to be obtained through single evaluation of the frozen teacher at the shifted input, rather than through computationally expensive Monte Carlo estimation requiring multiple teacher posterior samples. By varying the reweighting direction, PMD imposes family of constraints that uniquely characterize the teachers posterior under the stated assumptions. PMDs tilted-mean constraints uniquely characterize the teachers full conditional posterior at each fixed noisy input, under the stated assumptions. Importantly, modes missing from the students current outputs can remain visible to the objective, providing learning signal for recovering lost diversity. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: Direct posterior supervision. We formulate conditional distribution-matching objective based on exponentially tilted means. The tilt=shift identity makes these targets accessible through single frozen-teacher evaluation per tilt, avoiding expensive Monte Carlo sampling from the teacher posterior. Posterior identification and any-step sampling. We prove that, zero population loss uniquely identifies the full conditional posterior, including its multimodal structure and mode probabilities. An exact posterior student can then reproduce the target distribution without retraining. Superior Conditional Diversity. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD consistently outperforms competing methods in intra-prompt diversity across all evaluated metrics, while achieving the best FID among four-step methods. 2. Related Work Trajectory-Based Distillation. Progressive Distillation [48] merges consecutive denoising steps, while Consistency Models [54], Latent Consistency Models (LCM) [33], and LCM-LoRA [34] learn mappings to trajectory endpoints. Phased Consistency Models (PCM) [56] extend consistency learning to shorter trajectory segments, while SDXLLightning [28] combines progressive and adversarial distillation. Consistency Trajectory Models (CTM) [23] and flow-map methods [4, 14, 17, 47] learn transitions between arbitrary time pairs. Recent advances include Parallel Decoding Distillation [52], targeting interval-averaged velocities, flexible sampling budgets, and parallel prediction, respectively. On-policy approaches such as [7, 52, 64] imitate teacher velocities along student trajectories , while Simplified Matching Distillation (SMD) [64] combines on-policy velocity regression with training-time residual proxy and repulsion from weaker teacher predictions. Distribution-Based Distillation. Adversarial Diffusion Distillation (ADD) [51] and Latent Adversarial Diffusion Distillation (LADD) [50] use discriminator feedback for few-step generation. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [62] minimizes an approximate reverse-KL objective using teacher and auxiliary student score estimates, while DMD2 [61] improves this framework through twotimescale optimization, adversarial supervision, and multistep backward simulation. More recently, Reward-Tilted Distribution Matching Distillation (RTDMD) [22] combines distribution matching with reward-guided reinforcement learning to improve human-preference alignment in few-step generators. Alternative objectives include - divergence matching in f-distill [59] and Fisher-divergencebased distillation in Score Identity Distillation (SiD) [67]. In order to mitigate mode collapse, several works have combined distribution matching with trajectory matching techniques [16, 28, 62, 66]. Unlike methods that primarily align generated marginals, PMD directly targets the teachers full conditional posterior at each noisy input, providing supervision for preserving its multimodal structure. Conditional Posterior Modeling. DDMs [8] train stochastic denoisers to model conditional posteriors using proper scoring rules, while iDDM [37] improves their computational efficiency. Moment Matching (MM) [49] instead distills pretrained teacher by matching conditional means at re-noised student predictions, using either an auxiliary denoiser or parameter-space optimization. PMD shares the goal of posterior modeling but obtains supervision directly from frozen teacher through exponential tilting. Exponential Tilting. Under Gaussian corruption linear exponential tilt is equivalent to shifting the noisy input at fixed noise level [9, 42]. This connection has been exploited for reward-tilted sampling and alignment [40, 41] and for reward guidance in discrete diffusion models [38]. Related Gaussian-conditioning identities, in which the shift is accompanied by change of noise level or covariance, appear in transition sampling and inverse problems [20, 36]. Unlike flow-map methods that explicitly learn transitions between pairs of noise levels, PMD learns the conditional posterior of clean images at each noise level. During sampling, the student predicts clean image from the current noisy state. If another step is required, this prediction is re-noised to the next selected level using the Gaussian corruption schedule, and the student is evaluated again. The final prediction is returned without re-noising. Models and baselines. We evaluate Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD) on text-to-image models from two families: SDXL [45] and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B [27]. Our primary setting uses four sampling steps. For SDXL, we compare against LCM-LoRA [34], SDXL-Turbo [51], SDXLLightning [28], Flash [5], PCM [56], DMD2 [61], and Moment Matching [49], as well as an undistilled teacher reference. For FLUX.2 [klein] 4B, the comparison includes the base model, SMD [64], RTDMD [22], and Moment Matching [49]. The number of network function evaluations (NFE) is reported alongside generation quality to make the inference budget explicit. Implementation details. All experiments are conducted on 8 NVIDIA L40 GPUs for 2000 student updates, with batch size of 16. We use discriminator-to-generator update ratio of 5:1. We use 4 student draws per training state. We optimize with AdamW (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999), learning rate of 5 107, gradient norm clipping at 10, and fixed GAN loss weight of 0.75. We initialize the student from the undistilled pretrained model. To enable stochasticity, we concatenate Gaussian noise-mixed and original latent tokens, doubling the input projection dimension. Further architectural details are provided in the Appendix C. Evaluation metrics. We measure generation quality and prompt adherence using GenEval [15], DPG-Bench [21], OneIG-EN [6], HPSv3 [35], PickScore [24], and CLIP [46] Score (CLIP-S), and report FID [18] as an additional distributional quality measure. To assess intra-prompt diversity independently of prompt adherence, we use the Vendi score [12] and perceptual/feature-space diversity metrics based on LPIPS [65], DINOv2 [44], and DreamSim [13]. Metric details are shared in Appendix C.4. Qualitative Results. Fig. 5 provides qualitative comparisons of PMD against DMD2 on SDXL and RTDMD on FLUX.2 [klein] 4B under identical text prompts. Across both model families, PMD exhibits greater variation in subject appearance, scene composition, and backgrounds while preserving the semantic content of the prompts. The figure also demonstrates PMDs any-step capability: the same trained student generates diverse samples with four and two inference steps. Additional results are provided in Appendix G. Table 1 shows that PMD achieves the best FID among the compared four-step methods on both SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B, while leading in OneIG-EN and PickScore on SDXL and HPSv3, PickScore, and CLIP-S on FLUX.2. RTDMD [22], which uses additional external reward supervision, achieves GenEval, HPSv3, and PickScore scores of 0.9076, 15.59, and 23.99 on FLUX.2, but substantially worse FID of 31.57 compared to PMDs 24.12. Ablation on PMD Components As λ 0, the objective approaches ordinary mean matching, with limited sensitivity to covariance and higherorder posterior structure. Increasing the tilt radius strengthens the exponential reweighting, allowing PMD to probe Table 6 isolates the two terms of the student objective Lstudent = LPMD + γGANLGAN in the four-step FLUX.2 [klein] 4B setting. All variants use the same stochastic student architecture, so the differences are attributable to the Figure 10. User Study Form. training objective rather than to the noise input. PMD only. Removing the GAN loss yields the highest intra-prompt diversity on all four metrics, with Vendi score of 5.112 and DreamSim, DINOv2, and LPIPS diversities of 0.4843, 0.5873, and 0.6435. Relative to Stochastic DMD, this is roughly 2.0, 2.2, and 2.3 higher on Vendi, DreamSim, and DINOv2, respectively. The same variant has the weakest quality and alignment scores (ImageReward 1.232, CLIP-S 26.88, FID 56.13). This behavior is expected and follows from the target that PMD matches, rather than from an optimization failure. The Tilt=Shift Identity and the Posterior Identification Theorem assume an exact posterior-mean denoiser, so all PMD targets are evaluations of the frozen teacher at guidance scale 1; classifier-free-guided prediction is, in general, not the posterior mean of any fixed clean-image distribution under Gaussian corruption. The distribution identified at zero PMD loss is therefore the teachers unguided conditional posterior. Text-to-image teachers sampled without guidance are known to produce broad but low-fidelity and weakly prompt-aligned samples, and student that matches this posterior faithfully inherits both properties. The low ImageReward and CLIP-S of the PMD-only student thus reflect the unguided teacher distribution, and its diversity scores should be read together with these quality scores, since part of the measured variation comes from samples that the guided teacher would not produce. GAN only. Removing the PMD loss gives reasonable quality (ImageReward 0.849, CLIP-S 32.52, FID 34.19) but the lowest diversity on every metric (Vendi 2.219, DreamSim 0.1922, DINOv2 0.2080, LPIPS 0.4007). Although the student still receives an independent noise input, the discriminator scores each sample individually and provides no incentive to use that input to cover the posterior. The diversity of PMD therefore comes from the posterior-matching objective and not from the stochastic architecture alone. Stochastic DMD. Training the same stochastic student with the DMD objective gives the best quality (ImageReward 1.019, CLIP-S 32.86, FID 28.85), but its diversity is only marginally above the GAN-only variant (Vendi 2.572 vs. 2.219) and about half that of the PMD-only variant. This is consistent with the mode-seeking behavior of the reverseKL objective: making the student stochastic is not sufficient, and the objective itself must reward coverage of the conditional posterior. Discussion. The two terms of the PMD objective are complementary. The PMD loss supplies Figure 11. User Study for FLUX.2 [klein] 4B four-step models. coverage of the teachers conditional posterior, while the GAN loss, which compares student samples with real images under caption conditioning, supplies the fidelity and prompt alignment that the unguided posterior lacks. PMD on its own is therefore not intended as complete training objective: it requires an auxiliary loss to reach competitive visual quality, and we use the adversarial term for this purpose. Their combination gives the full fourstep FLUX.2 [klein] 4B model reported in the main paper, whose diversity lies between the two extremes of this ablation (Vendi 3.371, compared with 5.112 for PMD only and 2.572 for Stochastic DMD) while reaching competitive quality at guidance scale 1. The adversarial term thus trades part of the unguided posteriors breadth for realism, and the resulting student remains substantially more diverse than the DMD-trained one. F. User Study Details We conducted human evaluation with 50 participants to assess the perceptual quality of Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD) against three baselines: SMD, RTDMD, and FLUX.2 [klein]. The evaluation considered three criteria: diversity, realism, and prompt alignment. Evaluation Protocol. We selected 24 text prompts and generated four images per prompt using different random seeds, resulting in 96 images per method. For each prompt, the four generated images were presented together in an image grid, allowing participants to assess variation across samples conditioned on the same text description as shown in 10. Participants were asked to rate each image grid along three dimensions: 1. Diversity: How diverse are the generated images? 2. Realism: How realistic are the generated images? 3. Prompt alignment: How well do the generated images align with the provided text prompt? Each criterion was evaluated on five-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (Very Bad) to 5 (Very Good). For each baseline, we compared its ratings with those of PMD and computed the percentage of comparisons in which PMD received higher rating, an equal rating (tie), or lower rating. The aggregated results are presented in Fig. 11. Results. PMD substantially improves sample diversity, receiving higher ratings in 64%, 85%, and 66% of comparisons against SMD, RTDMD, and FLUX.2 [klein], respectively, while receiving lower ratings in only 6%, 3%, and 4%. For realism and prompt alignment, most comparisons result in ties, indicating broadly comparable performance. PMD shows its strongest realism advantage over RTDMD, winning 45% of comparisons versus 12% losses. Overall, these results demonstrate that PMD significantly enhances diversity while maintaining competitive realism and prompt adherence. G. Table 7 compares PMD against rCM, AnyFlow, DMD2, and PDD in terms of generation quality, semantic consistency, and sample diversity. We measure video quality using VBench and evaluate diversity through pairwise feature distances from V-JEPA 2 and VideoMAE V2 across five generated videos per prompt. Generation Quality. PMD achieves the highest VBench Semantic score of 82.04 and competitive Quality score of 86.33, resulting in an Overall score of 85.47, closely matching AnyFlows 85.51. Notably, PMD surpasses the 50-step teacher reference in all three VBench metrics while requiring only four network evaluations. These results demonstrate that PMD preserves semantic consistency and visual quality under substantially reduced sampling budget. Figure 12. Diversity and visual quality comparison on Wan 2.1 1.3B. Four-step generation results for the prompt woman in street across three noise seeds. DMD2 and AnyFlow produce visually similar facial structures and appearances across different seeds, indicating limited generative diversity, while rCM exhibits substantial degradation in visual quality. In contrast, our Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD) generates diverse facial identities, poses, clothing, and street backgrounds while maintaining high visual fidelity and prompt alignment. These results highlight PMDs ability to preserve sample diversity and generation quality under the same four-step sampling budget.
